# Jon Martin

> Jon Martin writes diagnoses of why systems and org structures keep breaking in founder-led professional services firms. He works in revenue operations — systems integration and subscription management, mostly for SaaS and professional services companies — and treats the job as variety management, not tooling. He also runs Portal Audit (https://audit.thejonmartin.com), a free HubSpot health check, automated via AI, that never changes anything in your portal unless you turn fixes on. The Four Laws of Complex System Design is his standing reference on the systems theory (Ashby, Conway, Brooks, the Reverse Conway Maneuver, Beer's Viable System Model) behind that diagnosis work. Requirements Altitude is the companion written guide for classifying discovery statements (L0–L3) so requirements stay scopeable.

Every public page on the site is listed below. Descriptions are taken from each page's own content.

## Main pages

- [Home](https://thejonmartin.com/): Portal Audit and Portal Fixer. A free HubSpot health check with a scored report and a 90-day plan. It never changes anything in your portal unless the customer turns on fixes (Fix plan, after dry run and approval). The checks apply Jon's own judgment through AI and automation: the best practices and issues he has seen over 11 years across B2B SaaS, B2B services, custom manufacturing, and companies that work inside and on top of HubSpot. For HubSpot admins at smaller companies and agencies or consultants who manage HubSpot for clients. The app is at [audit.thejonmartin.com](https://audit.thejonmartin.com).
- [About](https://thejonmartin.com/about): Who Jon is and what he does — revenue operations as variety management, why the deliverable is a written diagnosis rather than a project, where the Four Laws framework comes from, and Portal Audit.
- [Pricing](https://audit.thejonmartin.com/pricing): Portal Audit plans: a free audit (one per portal); Watch $19/mo; Fix free during beta, then $49/mo. No onboarding fee. thejonmartin.com/pricing 301s to audit.thejonmartin.com/pricing.
- [Tools](https://thejonmartin.com/tools): HubSpot-adjacent tool write-ups (Aircall, Apollo.io, Capsule and Transpond, Trainual, AdCreative.ai, Unitel Voice, Seamless.AI, WhatConverts, ElevenLabs, Gamma, Plesk, QuickSigner): what each does, how it fits a HubSpot stack, and where it doesn't. Pages contain affiliate links, disclosed on each page.
- [Writing](https://thejonmartin.com/writing): The essay archive — notes on org design, systems, and why the things you built keep breaking.
- [Requirements Altitude](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude): Written guide for classifying discovery statements at L0–L3 so scope stops being a pile of notes.
- [Contact](https://thejonmartin.com/contact): A short form for questions about the Four Laws framework or a correction to the site.

## Writing

- [Complex Isn't Complicated — And That Distinction Is Costing You](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/complex-isnt-complicated): Complicated systems have parts; complex systems have parts that adapt — which is why documentation alone stops working once a RevOps process scales.
- [Three Landscapes: Fuji, Rugged, and Dancing](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/three-landscapes): Scott Page's landscape metaphor for solvability — Mount Fuji, rugged, and dancing terrain — and why each shape calls for a different strategy.
- [The Interesting In-Between](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/interesting-in-between): Good complexity doesn't come from maximizing integration and data, or from minimizing for simplicity — it lives in the middle Page calls the interesting in-between.
- [Diversity, Deconstructed](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/diversity-deconstructed): "Diversity" isn't one thing — Scott Page breaks it into four distinct measures, and most "too much" or "too little" arguments are really about different ones.
- [Why Some Things Should Never Fully Ship](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/explore-exploit): Dancing landscapes call for an ongoing explore/exploit discipline, borrowed from metallurgy, that most RevOps orgs never build.
- [What Shows Up Without Anyone Designing It](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/emergence-and-networks): Half of what keeps a scaling RevOps org functioning was never designed by anyone — it emerged bottom-up, the way structure does in complex systems.
- [The Small Event That Wasn't Actually Small](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/feedback-and-cascades): Highly connected systems can quietly organize into a shape where an ordinary event triggers a cascading failure on its own.
- [Harnessing What You Can't Control](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/harnessing-complexity): A complex system can't be controlled the way a complicated one can — the real skill is recognizing it accurately and responding to match.
- [Two Fields That Never Talked to Each Other, Converging on the Same Physics](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/capstone-four-laws): Ashby, Conway, Brooks, and Beer's systems theory and Scott Page's complexity science never cited each other, yet converge on the same mechanisms.
- [A Field-Tested Stakeholder Communication Matrix](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/stakeholder-communication-matrix): A six-tier communication matrix for systems integration and subscription management engagements — detail level should track decision-making need, not seniority.
- ["I Want to Make Processes More Efficient" — What That Actually Means](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/what-more-efficient-actually-means): Operations is variety management, not efficiency work — four systems laws (Ashby, Conway, Brooks, Reverse Conway) that make an ambiguous job definable.
- [The Missing Middle of Discovery](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/missing-middle-discovery): Discovery fails in the gap between pain and configuration — requirements live at four altitudes, and the usable one almost never arrives in the client's words.
- [The Reset Is the Project](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/the-reset-is-the-project): Scope resets aren't vendor failure; they happen when a signed L2 requirement is quietly renegotiated in Slack, UAT, and one more edge case.
- [Coastline Scoping](https://thejonmartin.com/writing/coastline-scoping): A RevOps project has no single length — a published estimate is a length at a stated altitude, from named sources, against a stated reference.


## Tools

Affiliate links, disclosed on each page. Each page covers what the tool does, how it fits a HubSpot stack, and where it doesn't.

- [Aircall](https://thejonmartin.com/tools/aircall): Aircall is a cloud phone system with one of the deepest HubSpot calling integrations. What it logs, what it costs you in setup, and who should skip it.
- [Apollo.io](https://thejonmartin.com/tools/apollo-io): Apollo can fill your HubSpot with contacts fast. The two integrations, the push and write rules that matter, and the review score you should read before buying.
- [Capsule and Transpond](https://thejonmartin.com/tools/capsule-and-transpond): Capsule is a simple CRM and Transpond is its email tool. For most HubSpot teams that's a second CRM. Who they actually fit, and how the HubSpot sync works.
- [Trainual](https://thejonmartin.com/tools/trainual): Trainual turns SOPs into assigned training with tests and completion tracking. How I use it to roll out process changes so they stick, and where it falls short.
- [AdCreative.ai](https://thejonmartin.com/tools/adcreative-ai): AdCreative.ai makes banners, ad copy, and short video ads. For HubSpot teams it sits upstream of the CRM. What it does, who it fits, and what to set up first.
- [Unitel Voice](https://thejonmartin.com/tools/unitel-voice): Unitel Voice is a business phone service for solo founders and small teams. No HubSpot integration confirmed. Who it fits, who should look elsewhere, and why.
- [Seamless.AI](https://thejonmartin.com/tools/seamless-ai): Seamless.AI is a contact data tool with a HubSpot import and a Breeze Prospecting Agent link. The fine print and the governance questions to settle first.
- [WhatConverts](https://thejonmartin.com/tools/whatconverts): WhatConverts tracks calls, forms, and chats back to their marketing source. Its HubSpot link runs through Zapier. How the two flows work and where they break.
- [ElevenLabs](https://thejonmartin.com/tools/elevenlabs): ElevenLabs agents can read and write HubSpot records mid-conversation. It's an API build, not a toggle. The setup, the risks, and what to settle first.
- [Gamma](https://thejonmartin.com/tools/gamma): Gamma builds AI presentations, and its HubSpot app reads deal, account, and campaign data into decks. What it does, how access works, and a first test.
- [Plesk](https://thejonmartin.com/tools/plesk): Most SMB sites aren't hosted on HubSpot. Plesk is a control panel for running WordPress sites that still use HubSpot tracking and forms. Who it fits.
- [QuickSigner](https://thejonmartin.com/tools/quicksigner): QuickSigner is a simple, lower-cost e-signature tool. No native HubSpot integration found, so the connection is an API build. What it takes and who it suits.

## Requirements Altitude

- [Overview](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude): A written guide for classifying discovery statements at L0–L3 so scope stops being a pile of notes.
- [Module 1: The Problem — Why Smart People Still Miss the Middle](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-01): Why discovery can sound competent and still produce unusable requirements.
- [Module 2: The Altitude Model](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-02): L0 through L3: what each level commits to, who authors it, and how to tell them apart.
- [Module 3: The Diagnostic — Classifying Statements in Real Time](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-03): A ladder you can run live: note the speaker, then classify altitude without stopping the call.
- [Module 4: The Three Failure Modes, In Depth](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-04): Detail spelunking, altitude blindness, and bridge overuse — and why all three feel like progress.
- [Module 5: The L2 Bridge Rule](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-05): How to construct the missing-middle sentence, when to deploy it, and the overuse guardrail.
- [Module 6: The Advisory Layer — When a Correct Requirement Is the Wrong Requirement](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-06): Vertical traceability: a confirmed L2 can still fail the L0 it is supposed to serve.
- [Module 7: Multi-Stakeholder Altitude Mapping](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-07): Every statement has an altitude and a source. Conflict is not the same as a gap.
- [Module 8: Practice Drills](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-08): Tagging, translation, live-fire, and conflict-mapping drills with worked transcripts.
- [Module 9: Applying It in Discovery Calls](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-09): Before, during, and after the call: how the framework sits in a real discovery motion.
- [Module 10: From Tagged Notes to the Requirements Document](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-10): How tagged, sourced statements become a document a scoping team can actually use.
- [Module 11: The Four Levels of Design — Deliverables Mapped to Altitude](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-11): Wishlist, process map, functional spec, and configuration design — each at its altitude.
- [Module 12: Requirements Drift in Delivery](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-12): What happens after discovery when new statements arrive and L2 is treated as optional.
- [Module 13: Capstone](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-13): One end-to-end pass: tag, bridge, map stakeholders, trace vertically, write the document.
- [Module 14: Common Frameworks Mapped to Altitude](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-14): JTBD, user stories, epics, impact maps, and use cases read against L0–L3.
- [Module 15: Applying the Framework to Written and Asynchronous Sources](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-15): The same diagnostic on decks, tickets, Slack threads, and recorded walkthroughs.
- [Module 16: Recovery — Closing Gaps After the Fact](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-16): What to do when you notice a missing L2 after discovery is already supposed to be over.
- [Module 17: Special Conditions](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-17): Edge cases that change how the ladder runs without changing the altitudes themselves.
- [Module 18: Assessment and the Proficiency Model](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/module-18): Five proficiency levels and a capstone rubric for the written guide and any later course.
- [Appendix A: The Field Card](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/appendix-a): One-page call card: speaker, ladder, bridge, three tells, vertical check.
- [Appendix B: Facilitator Guide](https://thejonmartin.com/altitude/appendix-b): Sequencing, drill debriefs, and the resistance point that shows up in every cohort.

## Four Laws of Complex System Design — Reference

- [Full Reference](https://thejonmartin.com/four-laws-complex-system-design-full): The complete reference on Ashby's, Conway's, and Brooks's Laws, the Reverse Conway Maneuver, and Beer's VSM — how they interact and apply to team boundaries.
- [Glossary](https://thejonmartin.com/glossary): Definitions of every term used across the reference — Ashby's, Conway's, and Brooks's Laws, Reverse Conway, Team Topologies, Beer's VSM, Little's Law, and the Theory of Constraints.
- [FAQ](https://thejonmartin.com/faq): Direct answers on Conway's Law vs. Team Topologies, Brooks's Law under Agile, Little's Law for knowledge work, and WIP limits vs. the Theory of Constraints.

## Four Laws — Applied essays

- [Applied Examples: The Four Laws Across Revenue Teams](https://thejonmartin.com/applied-examples): Ten worked examples of Ashby's, Conway's, and Brooks's Laws applied to Marketing, Sales, CS, Finance, and RevOps in SaaS and professional services teams.
- [Managing Process: Flow & Constraints](https://thejonmartin.com/four-laws-flow-and-constraints): A walkthrough of Little's Law and the Theory of Constraints — how work actually flows through the team structure the first three laws create together.
- [Conway's Law and Your RevOps Team Structure](https://thejonmartin.com/conways-law-revops-team-structure): Why CRM, CPQ, and billing systems mirror the RevOps org chart, and how to redraw team boundaries around quote-to-cash using the Reverse Conway Maneuver.
- [Conway's Law in the AI Agent Era](https://thejonmartin.com/conways-law-ai-agents-revops): AI agents inherit your team boundaries, not just your tasks — why an AI SDR or billing-exceptions agent fails exactly where the org chart already had a seam.
- [Why Executive Decisions Stall on Client Projects](https://thejonmartin.com/stakeholder-decision-bottlenecks): Little's Law, Kingman's formula, and Weinberg's context-switching numbers applied to the steering committee — why the same sign-off takes six weeks.
- [AI, System 4, and Beer's VSM](https://thejonmartin.com/vsm-ai-system-4): AI can supercharge System 4 environmental scanning, but faster signals without a functioning System 5 just produce organizational paralysis, faster.
- [WIP Limits vs. the Theory of Constraints](https://thejonmartin.com/wip-limits-vs-theory-of-constraints): A WIP limit is a Kanban practice; the Theory of Constraints tells you where to put it — and why conflating them leaves throughput where it started.

## Four Laws — Interactive tools

- [Flow Formula Calculator](https://thejonmartin.com/flow-formula-calculator): Interactive calculators for Little's Law, Kingman's formula, and Weinberg's context-switching numbers — plug in engagement numbers to see what they predict.
- [Flow & Constraint Diagnostic](https://thejonmartin.com/part8-flow-diagnostic): A five-step guided diagnostic — enter WIP, throughput, and constraint details for a personalized Five Focusing Steps writeup.
- [Stakeholder Decision Stall Checklist](https://thejonmartin.com/stakeholder-decision-checklist): Check off what's true of a stalled engagement to see whether it's a Little's Law queue problem, a Kingman utilization problem, or Weinberg signal distortion.
